review.why: The PR changes the password update logic to require 'old_password' to be present and valid when 'password' is provided, whereas the original code allowed password changes without 'old_password' (treating missing 'old_password' as a failed verification). This removes the ability to change passwords without providing the old password, which is a behavior change users and API clients would notice.

findings.label: regression
findings.why: The new condition requires both 'password' and 'old_password' to be present before verifying the old password, so requests with a new password but no old_password now return 200 instead of 400, weakening the intended security check.

findings.label: regression
findings.why: The new condition requires both 'password' and 'old_password' to be present before verifying the old password, so requests with a new password but no old_password now return 200 instead of 400, weakening the intended security check.

doppel_guided.summary: The flattened condition accidentally allows password changes without providing the old password, turning a 400 error into a 200 success.

suspicions.claim: The PR changes the password update logic to require old_password when password is provided, whereas before old_password was optional if the user had no password set.
suspicions.trigger: Send PUT /api/me with Authorization: Bearer <token> and JSON body {"password": "newpass"} for a user who has no password set (password_hash is NULL). Observe that the request now returns 400 instead of 200 with updated user.
suspicions.evidence: Probe s1 sent PUT /api/me with password only for a user with no password set; base returned 400 and head returned 200, so the behavior changed opposite to the claim.

suspicions.claim: The PR changes the error condition so that providing an incorrect old_password now returns 400 even when the user has no password set, whereas before it would allow the password change without old_password.
suspicions.trigger: Send PUT /api/me with Authorization: Bearer <token> and JSON body {"password": "newpass", "old_password": "wrongpass"} for a user who has no password set (password_hash is NULL). Observe that the request now returns 400 instead of 200 with updated user.
suspicions.evidence: Probe s2 sent PUT /api/me with password and wrong old_password for a user with no password set; both base and head returned 400 with the same validation error, so no change occurred.
